title: Karna Upon Krishna's Chariot
story:
The court of Hastinapura watched Krishna take Karna onto his chariot, and the wonder of it followed him out of the city. Karna was the one warrior of the Kuru host who could stand against Arjuna — a man the whole city knew only as a charioteer's son — and Krishna, the Pandavas' friend, had come to the Kuru capital to plead for peace. To see those two side by side, in full view of every chief and servant of the court that counted Karna its own, was something no one there had ever expected.

The plea had failed. Duryodhana, who held the Pandavas' half of the kingdom and would not give it back, had refused every word that Krishna and the holy sages with him had spoken, and the earth now stood on the edge of war. Before he left the city Krishna had gone to the rooms of Kunti, mother of the Pandavas, and carried away her parting words for her sons; he had saluted her and walked round her in farewell. Now, at the edge of the royal quarter, he dismissed the Kuru chiefs who had followed him through the city — Bhishma, oldest and most honored of their line, at their head — and then he drew Karna up onto the chariot, took his kinsman Satyaki up behind them, and drove out through the gates.

After he had gone, the Kurus gathered and talked among themselves of what they had seen, and their talk was not of hope. "The whole earth, blind with folly, has been caught in the net of death," they said. And they said also: "By Duryodhana's madness, everything here is doomed."

On the road, Krishna and Karna spoke together at length. What passed between them on that stretch of open ground is not set down in this telling; what is known is that they rode on deep in talk while the light failed and the miles unwound beneath them, the chariot keeping pace with the conversation. When Krishna had said what he had come to say, he dismissed Karna, urged his horses to speed, and turned toward Upaplavya, where the Pandava camp lay. Daruka, his charioteer, held the reins, and the swift horses — quick as thought — seemed to drink the sky as they ran. They covered the long way like hunting hawks and brought Krishna back to the camp of the Pandavas, where the five brothers waited by their fires to hear what he had seen and done in the city of their enemies.

The messenger of peace rode in alone, having left behind him the one man of the Kuru side he had chosen to ride beside — and a city that already knew itself doomed.
reflection: Krishna leaves Hastinapura with Karna beside him — the one warrior of the Kuru side he treats as a companion rather than a foe — and returns alone, at the speed of the mind, as if the conversation had given him everything and nothing. The Kurus' parting words frame the whole embassy: the earth already entangled in the meshes of death, not by the gods, but by Duryodhana's folly.
tradition_note: The fuller account of the private conversation between Krishna and Karna — in which Karna's birth is revealed and the kingdom offered to him — follows in the sequel (Udyoga Parva 5.138–141); the present story follows the compressed reference in 5.137.
next_story_tease: But the secret Krishna had begun on that road — the truth of Karna's birth — had yet to be spoken aloud.
hero_scene: Krishna's chariot thunders out of Hastinapura with Karna seated beside him and Satyaki behind, the dust of the road rising as Bhishma and the Kuru chiefs stand watching at the city gates.
